chunks: How differential signals improve noise immunity. The question: How do they improve noise immunity?
Differential signaling resists noise because noise hits both wires of the pair almost equally, and the receiver only looks at the difference between them.
Equal noise on both wires cancels in that subtraction. The signal, which is opposite on the two wires, does not cancel. It adds up to double.
Hold a tape measure stretched between your two hands while riding a jolting train. Every bump lifts or drops both hands together, so the tape's length hardly changes.
The length is the message and the bumps are noise. This works only while both hands move together.
If one hand bounced more than the other, the length would change, and that is how real pairs leak noise.

Each leg carries a plus or minus 175 millivolts signal on top of a plus or minus 400 millivolts interference tone, so a single-ended receiver on either leg could not read the data (the noise is bigger than the signal).
The difference trace is a clean plus or minus 350 millivolts square wave: the interference is identical on both legs and drops out.
Noise: unwanted voltage picked up from nearby circuits, motors or radio waves.
Common-mode noise: noise that appears equally on both wires ("Common-mode voltage of a differential pair"). CMRR: how well a receiver rejects the part shared by both wires.
40 decibels means the shared part shrinks 100 times. Imbalance: one wire picking up more noise than the other. It turns some shared noise into a false difference.
Twisted pair: two wires twisted together, so both see the same interference.
Say 0. 5 volts of noise lands on both wires, while the real signal is a 0. 35 volts difference. A single wire would carry the full 0.
5 volts of noise, which is bigger than the signal. On a pair, the receiver subtracts the wires. If it has a CMRR of 40 decibels, a factor of 100, then 0.
5 volts / 100 = 5 millivolts of the noise leaks through. With 60 decibels (a factor of 1000), only 0. 5 millivolts does. Either way, the 0. 35 volts signal is far larger.
That is the whole idea: shared noise cancels and the signal does not.
"Noise couples about equally onto both wires of a closely routed pair, so it's common-mode, and the differential receiver subtracts it away.
The receiver's common-mode rejection ratio sets how well: 60 decibels turns half a volt of common-mode noise into half a millivolt.
Beyond that, the signal is twice as large, the threshold is the crossing of the two wires so it doesn't depend on ground or supply, and the equal and opposite currents don't disturb their own ground.
The limits are symmetry, skew and the receiver's common-mode range."
